analysis.one_liner: Lets Treasury clarify which workers count as employees for payroll taxes and toughens penalties for misclassification.
analysis.headline: Despite 117 House cosponsors, the bill received no hearing, markup, or vote and died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Since 1978, the IRS has been barred from writing rules that say who is an employee versus an independent contractor for payroll taxes, leaving a gray zone that some employers use to avoid withholding, Social Security and Medicare taxes, and to skip benefits. This bill would lift that ban, have Treasury issue clear rules with one-year transition, protect businesses that had a reasonable basis from retroactive tax bills, require firms to tell their contractors in writing what taxes they owe and what employee protections they lack, and end reduced penalties for firms that had no reasonable basis for treating workers as contractors. It never moved after being referred to the Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are really employees but are labeled independent contractors gain the protections employees have — unemployment insurance eligibility, workplace safety coverage, and possible benefits — plus clear written notice of their status and their right to ask the IRS for a ruling. Businesses that correctly pay employment taxes gain a level competitive field against rivals who cut costs by misclassifying. Treasury and honest taxpayers gain from shrinking the tax gap.

how_it_helps.text: The bill's findings state that misclassification denies workers unemployment benefits, workplace health and safety protections, and retirement or other employee benefits, and contributes to the federal and state tax gap.
It directs the Treasury Secretary to issue regulations and guidance clarifying the proper employment status of workers for employment tax purposes, ending a 32-year prohibition on such guidance.

It requires businesses that regularly hire independent contractors to give them written notice of their federal tax obligations, the labor and employment law protections that do not apply to them, and their right to seek a status determination from the IRS.
It eliminates the reduced penalty provisions for taxpayers who lack a reasonable basis for treating workers as independent contractors instead of employees.

It protects businesses from retroactive tax assessments on past misclassifications if they had a reasonable basis, relied on precedent or past audits, or followed long-standing industry practice, providing an orderly one-year transition to the new rules.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that classify workers as independent contractors without a reasonable basis would owe back employment taxes on future-determined cases and would lose the reduced-penalty provisions, raising their labor costs. Firms that relied for decades on the 1978-era safe harbor would face a one-year transition to new rules and the end of that safe harbor, plus a new paperwork requirement to notify contractors.

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals Section 530 of the Revenue Act of 1978, the safe harbor that protected businesses from misclassification liability for 32 years when they had a reasonable basis, and new guidance applies only one year after enactment, giving affected industries little time to adjust their business models.

The no-retroactive-assessment protection does not apply to skilled workers such as engineers, designers, drafters, computer programmers, and systems analysts, so those contractors and their clients could face tax bills for past periods under an arrangement with another person.

Businesses that genuinely use independent contractors would bear new compliance costs, including a written notice requirement to every regularly used contractor, and would face uncertainty about how Treasury's new guidance would classify their workers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core shift benefits workers who lose protections and honest competitors who pay their taxes, and it reduces the tax gap everyone else pays for. The design is deliberately careful: it protects past behavior when there was a reasonable basis, gives a one-year transition, and shifts the burden of proof to the IRS only when a taxpayer makes a prima facie case. The real cost falls on business models built around treating employees as contractors, which is the point of the bill, though the skilled-worker carve-out and the end of the long-standing safe harbor create genuine transition pain for some compliant small businesses.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim McDermott introduced the Fair Playing Field Act of 2010 on September 15, 2010, near the end of the 111th Congress.
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day; the action history shows no further action, no hearing, and no vote.
The bill attracted 117 cosponsors, all of them House Democrats, roughly in the three months before the Congress expired.

The bill would have repealed the 1978 ban on Treasury guidance on worker employment tax status, directed new guidance, provided transition relief from retroactive assessments, required notice statements to independent contractors, and eliminated reduced penalties for noncompliance without a reasonable basis.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that avoid payroll taxes and benefits by labeling employees as independent contractors kept the status quo — no IRS guidance and the 1978 safe harbor remained intact. Misclassified workers gained nothing.

for.name: Jim McDermott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Playing Field Act of 2010 in the House.

against.name: Sander Levin
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup after its referral; the committee took no action before the Congress ended.

against.name: Staffing and workforce-outsourcing industry groups
against.role: Businesses whose models depend on independent-contractor classification
against.what_they_did: Opposed misclassification enforcement legislation that would end the 1978 safe harbor and allow Treasury to reclassify their workers.

sides.party_line_note: All 117 cosponsors were House Democrats, with no Republican support on the bill itself; the Democratic chairman also took no action to advance it.

industries.note: These firms supply contract labor classified as independent contractors; new Treasury guidance and the end of the Section 530 safe harbor would force reclassification and employment tax liability on many of their placements. Their cost savings come largely from benefits and payroll taxes workers do not receive.

industries.industry: Businesses using independent contractors (construction, delivery, trucking, services)
industries.note: The bill ends reduced penalties and the safe harbor for firms lacking a reasonable basis, raising costs for those built on contractor labor, but protects firms with a reasonable basis from retroactive assessments and gives everyone a one-year transition. Workers misclassified by these firms lose unemployment and safety protections.

industries.industry: Compliant employers who pay employment taxes
industries.note: The bill's findings state misclassification creates inequities in competitive positions among businesses; clear rules and tougher penalties would level the field for firms that already withhold and pay payroll taxes.

The carve-out for engineers, designers, drafters, programmers, and systems analysts means these workers and their clients can still face retroactive tax assessments for past periods, even as the bill gives other contractors transition relief. On the other hand, clearer guidance could resolve long-standing ambiguity for legitimate contractors.
